Zero and First Conditional - Review

The Zero Conditional is used to talk about what you usually do in real-life situations. The result of the condition is always true according to the initial situation.
You use the First Conditional with if clauses to exchange opinions about possible future outcomes.

The Zero Conditional, also called the Present Real Conditional uses the following structure:
If/when … Simple Present, … Simple Present
or
Simple Present … if/when … Simple Present.

Both if and when are used in the Present Real Conditional. Using if suggests that something happens less frequently. Using when suggests that it is fairly certain the condition will be fulfilled.

You use the First Conditional to say it's possible that you will or will not do something. In that condition, something else may, may not, will, or will not happen. The outcome is not in the present, but in the future.

Structure:
If + Present Simple … will + verb …
or
will + verb .... + if + Present Simple

If people overeat, they become overweight.
If it rains on Saturday, I will stay home and watch a movie.
If you are too relaxed, they take advantage of you.
If you communicate clearly and honestly, it makes everything easier.
If you listen well too, people respond more honestly.
If this trip goes well, I'll come back with some ideas.
If you have any spectacular meals, will you get the recipes?
Perfect Infinitives - Review

You use the Perfect Infinitive to talk about an action that will be completed at a point in the future.
The Perfect Infinitive can refer to an action that was completed, or that was expected to be completed at some point in the past.
You use the Perfect Infinitives with modals must, might, could, may and can't to express a deduction or disbelief about something in the present or the past.
The modal you choose depends on the level of probability you want to express.

The Perfect Infinitive can refer to an action that will be completed, or that is expected to be completed at some point in the future.

You use the Perfect Infinitive to talk about future actions with verbs like expect, pretend, prefer, or hope.
Example:
She expects to have it done by 10 tonight.

You use the Perfect Infinitive to talk about past actions with verbs like expect, pretend, prefer, or hope.
Example:
She expected to have contacted everyone by the end of the evening.

You use the Perfect Infinitive with non-finite clauses to refer to events that have happened in the past, or events that should or might have happened but did not happen in the end.
A non-finite clause is introduced by a verb with no subject.

Example:
To have pulled that off is impressive.

You use must for logical conclusions. There is a strong degree of certainty about the present situation.

You use may, might and could to express a deduction about things in the present or the past when there are other possibilities or when the situation is possible but not certain. These modals have the same meaning.

You use can't when the situation is impossible or to express disbelief.

modal verb + have + past participle
It must have been difficult to pull that off.
I may have been too distracted to manage properly.
Because I'm British I might have seemed a little cold at times.

Bill: It must have been difficult to pull that off, Vanessa.
Vanessa: Well I didn't get much sleep, but I was eager to finish my course and get the restaurant management certificate. Now my goal is to improve customer relations and be a fair and caring manager.
Bill: You've been held accountable for everything at Bistro 88 lately, and it can't have been easy. You've also had a lot of repeat business. When I was manager I hated dealing with complaints and reprimanding the servers and I may have been too distracted to manage properly. If you are too relaxed, they take advantage of you. The customer complaints were also difficult to take.

Vanessa: Agreed. When I began to be more aware of the way I was presenting myself to the servers, I realized my non-verbal communication was the problem. I was really stressed and closed. It could have been a cultural bias too, in a way. Because I'm British, I might have seemed a little cold at times. Now I am always double-checking with the servers in order to really find out what the issues are. I think the success of the restaurant hinges on clear communication between everyone, including the staff and the customers. If you communicate clearly and honestly, it makes everything easier.
Bill: True. If you listen well too, people respond more honestly. Communication is always a challenge. I think you have the right attitude and personality to manage people. More wine?

Vanessa: Oh yes, just a little more, please. What about you Bill? Do you intend to invest in any other projects?
Bill: Not for the moment. If this trip goes well, I'll come back with some ideas. I hope to get inspired when I'm in the Maldives. What about you Vanessa? Do you intend to do any traveling in the near future, now that you have two weeks vacation?
Vanessa: Sure do! If you have any spectacular meals, will you get the recipes?
Bill: It would be my pleasure. Maybe you and I could think about opening a different kind of restaurant one day.
